terms.definition: AI systems, usually built on large language models, that produce text, code, images or other content from prompts. In enterprises it now spans assistive tools such as copilots through to autonomous agents.
A neural network trained on very large text corpora that can understand and generate language. Agents use LLMs as their reasoning engine.

AI systems in which agents, powered by LLMs, plan multi-step tasks, call tools and APIs, validate their own outputs and trigger actions in enterprise systems with limited human direction. Both sources treat it as the current frontier of enterprise AI.
A software component that uses an LLM to decide what to do next, can invoke tools, keep state or memory, and act on other systems. Several agents working together form a multi-agent system.

Coordinating several specialised agents (for example planner, extractor, validator, publisher) so they complete a workflow together. Emerging as the dominant design pattern for complex automation, though scaled production examples remain a minority.

An assistive AI application that helps a person do their job, such as drafting, summarising or answering questions, while the person stays in control. The first wave of enterprise GenAI was dominated by copilots.
AIM's family of GenAI work where the model helps a person or is embedded in an existing system: content generation, knowledge retrieval (RAG), model customisation and multimodal processing.
AIM's second family of GenAI work: multi-step tasks executed with planning, tool use and workflow automation. The fastest-growing segment.

An architecture where the system first retrieves relevant enterprise documents or data, then gives them to the LLM so its answer is grounded in that content. Now considered table stakes; the first pattern most enterprises adopt.
A RAG pattern in which retrieval, reasoning and action are orchestrated dynamically by an agent rather than in a fixed pipeline. Named as a differentiator once basic RAG is commoditised.
Combining vector (semantic) search with keyword search and a re-ranking step to improve retrieval quality in RAG systems.
A second-stage model that re-orders retrieved passages by relevance before they are passed to the LLM.
Splitting documents into passages for indexing and retrieval. Domain-specific chunking strategies are cited as a source of RAG quality differences.

A numeric vector representing the meaning of a piece of text (or image) so that similar items can be found by distance. Domain-specific embedding models are used to improve retrieval in specialised fields.
A datastore optimised for storing embeddings and finding nearest neighbours, used as the retrieval layer in RAG.
A structured network of entities and relationships that gives an LLM explicit facts and context. Used to augment RAG and reduce hallucination.
A layer that maps enterprise data, business rules, glossary terms and context into a form agents and LLMs can use consistently. Also called an enterprise context layer or ontology.
Pipelines that ingest documents, apply OCR, classify, extract fields and enrich metadata so unstructured content becomes usable by AI and downstream systems.
Models and pipelines that reason across text, images, audio and video, for example OCR plus LLM document digitisation.
Further training a foundation model on domain data so it performs better on specific tasks or language. Techniques include LoRA, QLoRA, RLHF and DPO.
Efficient fine-tuning methods that train a small set of extra parameters instead of the whole model, cutting cost and memory.
A training method that uses human preference judgements to steer model behaviour.
A simpler alternative to RLHF that optimises the model directly on preference pairs.

Adapting models to an industry's language and accuracy needs through fine-tuning, custom embeddings, prompt optimisation and domain evaluation sets. Deployed selectively where accuracy is business-critical.
Designing and tuning the instructions given to an LLM, including structured prompts, prompt libraries, versioning and automated optimisation.
Reducing the number of tokens sent to a model without losing meaning, to lower cost and latency.
Sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, reserving large models for complex reasoning. A core cost-control technique.
Reusing previously computed prompt context or answers so repeated requests cost fewer tokens.
Controls that constrain model inputs and outputs: prompt-injection and jailbreak defence, content moderation, PII redaction, bias and hallucination checks.
An attack where malicious text in the input or in retrieved content makes the model ignore its instructions. Input validation against it is part of LLMOps.
A prompt crafted to bypass a model's safety behaviour. Jailbreak prevention is listed alongside prompt-injection defence.
Deliberate adversarial testing of a model or agent to find failure modes before deployment.
A confident but false or unsupported model output. Cited as the challenge that most directly erodes enterprise trust, worse in production than in controlled pilots.
Requiring the model to attach source references to its statements so outputs are traceable to documents. A common response to hallucination in regulated settings.
Attaching a confidence estimate to each output so low-confidence answers can be routed to human review.

Design pattern where a person reviews, approves or corrects AI outputs at defined checkpoints. Used both to manage risk and to build user trust incrementally. Cited by 33 percent of IDC respondents as a top barrier to scaling agents.
A control in which one party produces an output and a second independently checks it before it is accepted. Applied to agent and analyst workflows in regulated finance.
An agent whose job is to check another agent's output for factuality, citation completeness or policy compliance and grade its confidence.
Using a language model to score the quality of another model's outputs at scale, as part of an evaluation framework.

Building GenAI systems with automated quality benchmarks and ground-truth test sets embedded through the build cycle and kept running in production, rather than one-time testing. A trait of vendors with high pilot-to-production conversion.

The operational discipline for GenAI systems: CI/CD with prompt and model versioning, monitoring, drift and hallucination tracking, cost and token control, security and audit logging. Described as the layer where production viability is decided.
The established practice of deploying and operating machine-learning models; LLMOps extends it for language models and AgentOps for agents.
Monitoring, governance and lifecycle management specific to AI agents: tracing agent actions, enforcing policies, evaluating behaviour and controlling execution.
End-to-end visibility into a GenAI pipeline: tokens, cost, latency, accuracy and agent traces, with feedback loops into improvement.
Detecting when model behaviour, data or retrieval quality changes over time so systems can be retrained or retuned.
Financial operations discipline applied to cloud and AI spend: real-time cost tracking, budgets and optimisation. Named as a required control for production GenAI.
Running AI systems with the same reliability engineering rigour as other production services: SLAs, incident response, capacity and cost management.
An open protocol that standardises how agents connect to tools and data sources. Several vendors name MCP hosting or gateways in their agent platforms.
A protocol for agents built on different frameworks to discover and communicate with each other. Relevant to the barrier of managing agents across frameworks.
The ability of an LLM or agent to invoke functions, APIs or enterprise systems as part of completing a task.

An agent reasoning loop that alternates between thinking about the next step and taking an action, then observing the result. One of the common agent design patterns alongside plan-and-execute and reflection.
An agent pattern that first produces a full plan and then executes its steps, in contrast to ReAct's step-by-step loop. Reflection adds a self-review step.
Turning a natural-language question into a database query so business users can ask questions of structured data. Underpins conversational BI products.
Natural-language interfaces over dashboards and data warehouses that answer questions and generate narrative insights.
Simulated customer segments generated by AI, used to test product concepts, messaging or pricing before real-market research. An emerging product category among service providers.
Artificially generated data used for training, testing or privacy-preserving analysis.
A simulation model of a business process or network used to run what-if scenarios. Some providers pair it with agents for risk and operations planning.
A domain command centre that combines monitoring, prediction, agent recommendations and workflow execution, typically for supply chain or finance operations.

A reusable, pre-built asset a service provider brings to engagements: RAG kits, agent frameworks, evaluation libraries, dashboards, domain templates. Vendors typically disclose 5 to 10; most are point solutions rather than integrated platforms.
A delivery model built around a vendor's own integrated platform rather than bespoke builds. Vendors with individually named platform components show higher productisation maturity.
A central team that standardises practices, maintains reusable assets and drives adoption of AI across an organisation, whether inside an enterprise or a service provider.
An engineer who works inside the client's environment to turn business needs into deployable solutions, bridging technical and business teams. Associated with better pilot-to-production conversion.
Building solutions jointly with the client, in their environment, on their data and platforms, iterating toward production. Cited as improving adoption and continuity.
A joint development engagement model used for strategic or complex initiatives, also used for vendor-to-platform partnerships.

The drop-off between GenAI pilots and systems that reach governed production use. Named the defining fault line of the market: most vendors convert 25 to 45 percent of pilots and industry pilot failure exceeds 70 percent. Causes are mostly organisational (governance, talent, change, compliance) rather than model quality.
A short, fixed-price proof of concept (two to four weeks) designed to validate value before a scale commitment.

Whether enterprise data is clean, consistent, documented and context-rich enough for GenAI. The gap between data that exists and data that is RAG-ready is the largest technical friction point, and data quality is the top technical challenge in the IDC survey.

The organisational work of getting people to trust and use AI systems: workflow embedding, role-based enablement, incremental trust building. Broadly under-invested; adoption failure is called the primary ROI risk.
The commercial structure of a services contract: project-based, capacity-led (pods), run-and-operate (managed services), outcome-linked, platform subscription, or co-innovation.
Billing by effort and hours rather than by fixed scope or outcome. Still the default for most GenAI engagements.
Tying part of a vendor's fee to measured business results. Rare but rising; only a few vendors in the AIM study offer it.
Ongoing operation of deployed AI systems by the vendor: monitoring, prompt tuning, knowledge refresh, retraining, support. The fastest-growing engagement model as production deployments increase.
Outsourced analyst and research work. Vendors with KPO roots tend to keep large standing benches of domain specialists who now work alongside agents.

A large standing pool of industry specialists who take part in fine-tuning, output validation and quality assurance. One of two models for bringing domain expertise into delivery; the other draws SMEs from a shared pool as needed.

AIM Research's vendor evaluation framework. Vendors are scored 0 to 1 on Penetration (market reach) and Maturity (delivery depth) and placed into four quadrants: Leaders, Seasoned Vendors, Growth Vendors, Challengers.
AIM's market-reach axis: delivery scale, financial health, growth, customer confidence, client reach and partnerships.
AIM's capability axis: work delivery, technical advancement, value realisation, team maturity and support infrastructure.
IDC's four percentile groups (Emerging, Developing, Advanced, Leaders) based on a 0 to 100 composite of real-time deployment depth, agentic AI adoption and measurable outcomes.
IDC's 0 to 100 score per respondent. Tier averages: Emerging 35, Developing 50, Advanced 60, Leaders 74.
Data that is captured, moved and made available as events happen rather than in batches. IDC's survey finds it is now treated as core infrastructure for agentic AI.
A design in which systems publish and react to events (state changes) as they occur, typically through an event broker or mesh. The basis of real-time data platforms.

A single, integrated platform for real-time data instead of many loosely connected tools. IDC calls consolidation onto one the clearest marker of a leader: 71 percent of Leaders versus 8 percent of Emerging organisations.
An accumulation of overlapping, loosely integrated tools that raises complexity and cost. Cited by 37 percent of IDC respondents as a top technical challenge.
Older systems and accumulated shortcuts that make integration and real-time data harder. A top-five technical challenge for buyers and a recurring integration challenge for vendors.
In the IDC survey, the share of an organisation's AI projects that deliver measurable outcomes. Averages range from 34 percent (Emerging) to 67 percent (Leaders).
IDC's short, sponsored research format that presents survey findings for external distribution.
The industry grouping most often named by service providers as a focus and the deepest area of GenAI domain specialisation.
Fast-moving consumer goods companies, frequently paired with retail in vendor focus areas.
Extracting figures from financial statements into a standard format for credit analysis. A common production GenAI use case in banking.
Standardised investor questionnaires whose drafting is a frequent GenAI use case in asset management.
The compliance review of pharmaceutical promotional content. Named as an agentic workflow in life sciences.
Monitoring and assessing adverse drug effects. Cited as a reasoning-heavy workflow where multiple agents validate each other's outputs.

terms.expansion: Good Practice regulations; US FDA electronic records rule
terms.definition: Life-sciences quality and electronic-records regulations that GenAI systems in pharma must satisfy for validation, auditability and traceability.
Common compliance standards (US health privacy, service-organisation security controls, EU data protection) that vendors cite as baseline requirements for production GenAI.
Automatically finding and masking personal data in inputs, outputs and training data, a standard governance control.
Restricting what each user or agent can see and do according to its role. Applied to agents as well as people in mature deployments.
A compact model used for high-volume, lower-complexity tasks to cut cost and latency, with large models reserved for hard reasoning.
A model trained to work through multi-step problems before answering. At least one service provider in the AIM study has released its own.

Designing, training and running AI under a country's own laws, on infrastructure it controls, with locally governed data, so that critical capability does not depend on foreign vendors. In 2025 most large companies treated data residency and a vendor's country of origin as planning inputs.
A requirement that data, and often the compute that processes it, stay within a named country or region. A core component of sovereign AI planning and a driver of local hosting decisions.

Where an AI product or model was developed and is hosted, used as a criterion when choosing vendors. Three quarters of Deloitte's respondents weigh it; Americas firms rely far less on foreign-sourced stacks than EMEA firms.

AI systems that sense the physical world, decide and act through machines or control systems: robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, automated machinery and the digital twins that model them. Adoption leads in controlled settings such as factories and warehouses and in Asia Pacific.

An industrial robot designed to work alongside people rather than in a caged cell. Cobots were about 14 percent of industrial robot installations in 2024 and are one of the physical AI types expected to have the greatest impact.

The distance between employees having sanctioned AI tools and actually using them in daily work. Deloitte found access rose by half in a year while daily use stayed flat, and names activation rather than availability as the main barrier to value.

The pattern in which organisations keep funding cheap, low-risk pilots instead of doing the harder work of scaling proven ones, because production needs integration, security review, compliance, monitoring and maintenance that pilots avoid. Timelines estimated at three months can stretch to eighteen.

A flatter, non-hierarchical team model considered by half of large companies because AI reduces the number of roles that supervise large teams. Only a small minority had adopted it to a great extent by late 2025.
Broad workforce literacy in using AI tools well. The most common talent response to AI (educating employees) but, on its own, far short of redesigning roles, workflows and career paths.
Structured programmes to raise employees' AI skills or move them into new roles. BCG's Trailblazer CEOs devote about 60 percent of AI budget to it, more than double other CEOs.

BCG's clustering of CEOs by AI investment, upskilling, personal AI expertise, state of mind and confidence. About 15 percent Trailblazers invest decisively and upskill most of the workforce, about 70 percent Pragmatists invest where value is evident, and about 15 percent Followers lack conviction.
The share of an organisation's change or transformation spending allocated to AI. Trailblazer CEOs commit about three quarters of it to AI, versus about a quarter for other archetypes.

Reshaping whole workflows and functions with AI rather than adding AI to individual tasks. BCG frames it as the step between everyday task use and inventing new business models; McKinsey's high performers redesign workflows at three times the rate of others.

Explicit rules about which decisions an agent may take on its own and which need human approval. Governance is expected to change as agent autonomy rises; Deloitte and KPMG describe boundaries, thresholds and override triggers as the mechanism.

Incentives that reward employees for consuming as many AI tokens as possible, sometimes tracked on internal leaderboards. Two in five large US firms would consider it; KPMG warns that usage-based incentives can reward the wrong behaviour when not tied to outcomes.

A cap on how much model usage a team, application or agent may consume, set to control AI operating cost. In place at about a third of large US firms in mid-2026; one in five organisations globally has already limited AI use because of operating costs.

The ability to see the full operating cost of AI systems, including tokens, inference, storage and compute, in real time. Only a quarter of large US firms had full visibility in mid-2026 despite most having dashboards and approval-stage cost reviews.

A defined condition under which a person overrides an AI output: a regulatory conflict, a confidence score below a limit, a breached risk threshold, or a business judgment that differs. A third of firms still override case by case without formal criteria.

A named C-suite executive accountable for AI outcomes. Accountability for AI-informed decisions is split between such named executives and the CEO or executive committee, with governance committees rarely the owner.
A short, frequently repeated survey of a fresh sample each wave. Quarter-over-quarter changes compare different respondents, so they are noisier than a panel would be.

Menlo's split of generative AI spend: applications (horizontal, departmental and vertical products people use) and infrastructure (model APIs, model training and the data and orchestration layer). In 2025 the two halves were almost equal at about $19B and $18B.

General-purpose AI applications that raise productivity across all functions, such as enterprise chat copilots, agent platforms and note-taking tools. The largest and fastest-growing application category in 2025, dominated by copilots.
AI applications built for a specific job role or function, such as coding, sales, customer success or HR. Coding was more than half of departmental spend in 2025.
AI applications built for a specific industry, such as healthcare, legal or government. Healthcare took about 43 percent of vertical spend in 2025, led by ambient clinical scribes.

A go-to-market motion where individual users adopt a product first and enterprise contracts follow. About a quarter of AI application spend arrives this way, four times the rate in conventional software, and near 40 percent when employee-paid tools are counted.

Employees using personal or unsanctioned AI tools for work, often paid for themselves and outside IT approval. Reported at more than 90 percent of companies against 40 percent with an official subscription, and a reason official tools are judged harshly.

The choice between purchasing an AI application and building on raw models in-house. Five sources converge on buying: purchased use cases rose to about three quarters, bought solutions reach production at twice the rate of internal builds, and enterprises are migrating from DIY to packaged apps. McKinsey adds a counter-current: a third have declined a software purchase because coding agents let them build it.
An AI application that listens to clinical encounters and drafts documentation, cutting documentation time by more than half. The largest healthcare AI product category in 2025 at about $600M.

An AI system that plans and executes multi-step software changes, beyond line-level code completion. Coding agent spend grew from near zero to about $1.1B in 2025; about a fifth of organisations were scaling coding agents by mid-2026.

A model whose weights are published for anyone to run, such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen or DeepSeek. Enterprise share of open models fell to about 11 percent by late 2025 as preference swung to closed frontier models, while startups and independent developers adopted Chinese open models quickly.

Designing what information, tools and memory a model receives for each task, as a successor to prompt engineering. Still niche in production (about 6 percent of enterprise deployments) but one of the fastest-growing skills in job postings.

Menlo's taxonomy of production systems: fixed-sequence, routing-based and single-shot workflows wrap one or more model calls in predetermined logic; multi-agent, single-trajectory and multi-trajectory agents let the model plan, act, observe and adapt. Only 16 percent of enterprise deployments were true agents in late 2025.

The expectation that total AI spend keeps rising even as the price per token falls, because usage volume grows faster than prices drop. Both Menlo and McKinsey use it to explain why AI is not becoming too cheap to meter.
The share of an enterprise's model spending that goes to each vendor. a16z's Global 2000 respondents put OpenAI at a majority but shrinking, with Anthropic and Google gaining.

Running several model families in testing or production and routing tasks to the best one. Four in five large enterprises use three or more model families, and routing across models has largely replaced fine-tuning in enterprises.

A model developer training the most capable models, such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. Enterprise trust in labs rose sharply: about four in five now host models directly with a lab rather than only through a cloud provider.

terms.term: Direct hosting with a frontier lab
terms.definition: Consuming a model from the lab's own service rather than through a hyperscaler marketplace. Rose from about 40 percent to about 80 percent of large enterprises between March 2024 and January 2026, a signal of rising trust in labs.

The effort and risk of moving from one model or tool to another once it is embedded in workflows or has learned from an organisation's data. Rising switching costs favour early footholds and learning-capable systems.
Return on AI spend expressed as a multiple of cost. In January 2026 half of large enterprises reported break-even (1x) or worse on LLM spend and 44 percent did not measure ROI precisely.

A survey whose respondents are recruited from a research vendor's database by screening criteria rather than random sampling. Results can over-represent advanced adopters and are not representative of the wider market.

MIT NANDA's term for the gap between the few organisations whose GenAI systems are integrated, learn from feedback and produce measurable impact, and the majority that have adopted general tools without structural change. The report's headline is that about 5 percent of custom task-specific tools reached sustained impact within six months in its sample.

NANDA's diagnosis of why enterprise AI tools stall: they do not retain feedback, remember context or adapt to workflows, so users reject them in favour of consumer tools. Two thirds of executives want systems that learn from feedback and retain context.
A frontline employee who already uses AI heavily and can lead adoption. NANDA finds successful buyers source initiatives from such users and line managers rather than a central AI lab.

NANDA's 0-to-5 composite of incumbent share volatility, AI-native revenue growth, new business models, changed user behaviour and AI-driven reorganisations. Most sectors scored near zero in mid-2025; media, telecom and technology scored highest.

NANDA's forward thesis of interoperable agents on protocols such as MCP, A2A and NANDA that discover vendors, form integrations and transact across organisations. A research position from the report's authors, not a survey finding.

Microsoft's label for organisations that learn fastest from their own AI use and encode what agents reveal into shared routines. A marketing frame that leads to Microsoft's advisory content; the underlying survey data is more reusable than the label.

In Microsoft's 2026 survey, an AI user who reports advanced agent use for multi-step work, routine workflow redesign and participation in repeatable AI practices. About 16 percent of AI users; a different construct from the 19 percent 'Frontier zone' of the readiness index.

Microsoft's finding that AI users fear falling behind yet feel safer optimising current goals than redesigning work, because reinvention is rarely rewarded when results do not follow. One in ten AI users is ready but blocked by an unready organisation.

Microsoft's term for an organisation that captures, evaluates and diffuses what agents reveal about its work, with evaluation infrastructure that scales alongside agents. Organisational AI culture explained about twice as much reported AI impact as individual factors.

Whether employees feel safe proposing new ways of working with AI and experimenting without penalty. Leaders report it far more often than employees do, and manager modelling of AI use is associated with materially higher reported AI value.

Treating each AI agent like a user account with permissions, policy, lifecycle management and audit, so that unauthorised access, unintended actions and data exfiltration can be controlled. Microsoft's prescription for IT and security teams; McKinsey finds a third of organisations already mitigating unintended agent action.

A respondent attributing at least 5 percent of EBIT to AI and describing AI's value as significant. About 6 percent of McKinsey's 2026 sample, unchanged from 2025; the strictest leading-group definition in this project.

terms.term: Phases of AI use (experimenting, piloting, scaling)
terms.definition: McKinsey's stages of deployment. In 2026, 44 percent of AI users were at least scaling, and large enterprises were far ahead of smaller ones on scaling agents.

A respondent's own estimate of the share of earnings before interest and tax attributable to AI. About 37 percent of organisations attribute any EBIT impact, flat year on year, while 80 percent report personal productivity gains.

The economics of paying per token for model usage. Unit prices fall but tokens consumed rise faster, especially for agentic coding and reasoning on frontier models, so operating cost has become a design constraint that heavy users feel first.
A central team with authority to remove bottlenecks across an AI programme. One of McKinsey's high-performer practices, though the gap to other organisations is small on this one.

The risk that an autonomous agent takes an action outside its mandate, such as making a purchase, sending a message or changing a system. The first agent-specific risk measured in a major survey: a third of organisations mitigate it, 45 percent among high performers.

Fundamentally changing how work is done around AI rather than adding AI to existing steps. The strongest single differentiator of leading organisations across sources: about 73 percent of McKinsey's high performers versus 25 percent of others, while 84 percent of Deloitte's respondents had not redesigned jobs.

Capital flowing into AI companies through mergers and acquisitions, minority stakes, private investment and public offerings, as tracked by Quid. Reached about $582B in 2025, of which private investment was about $345B; distinct from enterprise spend on AI products.

The share of a working-age population that uses AI tools, as opposed to the share of organisations that use AI. Generative AI reached about 53 percent of US adults within three years, faster than the PC or the internet; diffusion correlates with GDP per capita.

The value users get from a product above what they pay, estimated from what they would need to be paid to give it up. US consumer surplus from generative AI was estimated at $172B a year in early 2026, far above producers' revenue.

The pattern in which a general-purpose technology depresses measured productivity while firms invest in complements (skills, processes, data) and then raises it later. Used in the AI Index to reconcile strong micro-level gains with small aggregate effects so far.

A job whose tasks overlap heavily with what current AI can do. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations fell about 16 percent relative to the least exposed by late 2025, while older cohorts grew.

Whether an AI system completes a task on its own (automation) or works alongside a person (augmentation). In Anthropic's telemetry the two were roughly balanced through 2025, with automation briefly ahead in August; the split is one vendor's conversation mix, not a market measure.

The difference between AI experts' and the general public's expectations. In the US, 73 percent of experts but 23 percent of the public expect AI to improve how people do their jobs, and the public expects slower progress than experts in about seven of ten forecasts.

IDC's label for a period in which AI moves from assisting people to acting autonomously across the enterprise. IDC predicts half of enterprises will use agents to redefine human-machine collaboration by 2027 and that agentic systems will be nearly half of AI spending by 2029; both are forecasts.
